provenance: PR #29 R21. Three times in this PR a published wall-clock band failed to match the `evals/report/history.jsonl` committed beside it: nine of fifteen runs published as 'every run the ledger records', four values that appear in no recorded run at that case count, the two slowest `invariant` runs dropped unlabelled, and a ceiling derived from a maximum (64.71s) that was never measured. Nothing graded any of it, which is why prose drifted that far — and the same selective-band presentation is what ADR-013 Decision 4 was withdrawn over. This grades the PROPERTY, not the snapshot: `history.jsonl` grows on every gate run, so a check that string-matched the published list would go red on the next run rather than on a regression. It asserts that the doc's case count is the current one, that the committed ceiling is at least ADR-013's rule applied to the ledger's slowest run at that count, and that the published number derives that same ceiling. The last one is deliberately `rule(published) == rule(ledger max)` rather than the stricter `published >= ledger max` the reviewer proposed: the harmful failure R21 found is a band that justifies a LOWER ceiling than the truth (12.96s published where 13.57s was recorded, giving 15 where the rule said 20), and the strict form reddens on ordinary variance instead — this tree moved 0.2-0.5s between consecutive runs while the check was being written, which would make the doc need re-editing after every slightly slow run. That is the same rot-by-construction trap in a different place, so the property graded is the one that matters. T-R34 added two halves to the same check, both from the drift that produced that task: README's band-table row must carry the SAME case count and maximum as ADR-019's sentence (the two documents drifted apart in PR #29 R24 and only the ADR was graded), and a suite may publish exactly one band line -- the parse is a dict comprehension over `finditer`, so a superseded line left in the file used to shadow the live one in silence. PR #35 R2 and R4 added the two halves the round-1 version still missed: README's row parse was the same last-wins dict comprehension the ADR side had just been guarded against (stale rows ABOVE live rows left it green with two contradictory bands per suite), and nothing read the ceiling the ADR DERIVES in prose -- so a band re-measured downwards after a case was added could argue `-> **15**` under a heading that says 20s. The derivation sentence must now multiply the published maximum, be arithmetically right, and land on `WALL_BUDGET_S[suite]`. PR #35 R5 added the third: the published number must BE a row in the ledger recorded with nothing uncommitted in the tree (`dirty: false`). Round 1 published both bands off runs that were red AND dirty -- a band justified by a tree that was never committed. Green is deliberately NOT required and cannot be: this check is in both suites, so at a new case count every run is red until the band is republished and no green row could ever exist to republish it from (T-R53 carries that half). `evals/run.py` had to be fixed in the same round for a clean row to be producible at all -- `dirty` was read AFTER the report file was written, so every `--report` run recorded itself as dirty on account of its own untracked artifact. PR #35 R11 then found the `dirty: false` requirement deadlocked the one operation CLAUDE.md rule 2 makes routine: a tree only reaches count N+1 while the new case is uncommitted, so every row at N+1 is dirty until the commit the check was blocking. The band sentence now cites its run by ledger timestamp and cleanliness is judged AS OF that run -- a dirty row is refused only when a clean one was already available when the band was published. That is stable in both directions: it cannot deadlock the bootstrap, and later clean rows cannot retroactively redden a published band. R13 added the derivation's precision and the requirement that the stated arrow is `_band_rule(x)`; the separate claim that the ADR's advertised ceiling is the committed one moved to the Ruling line, because the rule applied to a fresh short sample legitimately comes out below the committed ceiling (12.89s at 53 cases gives 15 against a committed 20) and tying them together would have re-created R11's deadlock by another route. T-R56 folded two more properties into the same check, both from the same class of defect — a document describing a rule the code does not implement. T-R55: the `fast` band cited a row the ledger records as 134/136 and said nothing about it, while `invariant`'s citation disclosed 53/53, so a reader comparing the two would read the silence as a pass. The band sentence now carries the cited row's own `passed/total` and item 2 grades it — green is still required nowhere, which is exactly why the result has to be stated. T-R46/T-R47: §6 claimed to be the one place the rules are stated while two of its own paragraphs restated item 2, README restated items 3 and 7, and two keys this check's sibling emits were still on the `property N` numbering PR #35 round 4 retired — an off-by-one against §6's list in a red report. The restatements now defer by number and item 8 grades that the deferrals resolve: the list is 1..N with no gaps, and every `item N` in ADR-019, README or the check's own source names one of them, under that name. That is the structural half — a blacklist of retired phrases cannot catch a restatement that is correct today and stale next round, but a reference that stops resolving is red. PR #36 R1 then falsified the claim this section had been making about itself: 'one list, in one place ... stated nowhere else' was asserted in ADR-019, INDEX.md and this check's docstring while the same commit added restatements to all three. The claims are narrowed to what item 8 (references) actually grades — every reference names an item that exists and spells its slug — and the residue (an unreferenced paraphrase) is stated as ungraded rather than denied. PR #36 R10/R11 then found the narrowed claim overstating in turn: the Graded half promised a reference 'names an item that exists AND spells its slug' while a bare name for a nonexistent item was green, and promised the list carried slugs while a slugless trailing item was invisible. Both are graded now, and §6's Graded paragraph is written clause by clause against the mutations that hold it up. T-R44 added item 9 (environment), the ninth property and the first one that is about WHICH LEDGER the other eight read. ADR-019's Ruling had said "one per (suite, environment)" all along; this check had no environment dimension, so on CI — where the `invariant` step appends its own row to the job's copy of `history.jsonl` before the `fast` step grades §3's band against it — a band measured on a laptop was reddened by a run from another machine, green locally on the same tree (PR #32 CI run 32626835735; root-caused on `task/M32` as T-M32-13). The clause that fired was item 2 (cited-run)'s dirty allowance and the mechanism was `ts`, not the wall clock: `ts` was naive local time compared as a string, so CI's row followed the band row by 25 minutes and sorted eight hours before it, and being clean it satisfied "a clean row was already available by then". Isolated by its control — same row, same wall clock, same `dirty: false`, only the `ts` moved later, green. CI's wall clock entering `slowest`, which item 3 (same-ceiling) and item 4 (committed-ceiling) both read, is the OTHER symptom and it is not latent: it is what fired on T-R44's own origin run, 32626835735 (sha `434a98d`), where a published 12.92s against CI's 16.02s derives 15 against 20 and item 3 (same-ceiling) went red. That tree had no dirty clause at all, so nothing else could have. Only item 4 (committed-ceiling) stayed green there — 20 against `rule(16.02)` = 20 — and it is item 4 (committed-ceiling) alone that would need 17.39s to go red, a bound that does not apply to item 3 (same-ceiling). Item 9 (environment) closes both symptoms; the ordering key is fixed separately in the same change — `evals/run.py` `stamp()` is UTC, graded by `ledger-ts-orders-real-time`. Two properties, two fixes, neither standing in for the other (ADR-019 §7; T-M32-13 closed on the pair). Every history row now carries an `env` tag and the band sentence names the environment it was measured in; a row with no tag reads as `local`, which is what every row written before T-R44 is. The defect is pinned by two cases, one per property: `band-is-graded-against-its-own-environment` drives `_band_wrong` with a synthetic two-environment ledger, because the committed one holds no CI row and cannot (T-R51), and `ledger-ts-orders-real-time` grades the stamp under two explicitly-set zones. T-R60 (P1) closed here 2026-08-28, both halves, both watched red with the block's own mutations. (1) `_ADR_CEILING` built a LAST-WINS dict, so a second bolded ``local `fast` … **Ns**`` phrase anywhere in ADR-019 silently overrode the Ruling line item 6 (ruling) grades and INDEX digests — the same shadowing class already guarded for band lines and README rows (PR #29 R24, PR #35 R2), and the same shape as `adr_publishes_two_bands`, so it gets the same answer: two is a refusal, not a preference. Red on a planted `**999s**`: `{adr_publishes_two_ruling_ceilings: [120, 999]}`. (2) item 5 (derivation) searched the WHOLE file, so §6's counterexample — a paragraph that exists to call a state a residue — could satisfy it for a band with no derivation in its own section at all, and §5's CI sentences were kept out only by their multiplicands, which is luck rather than a rule. Derivations are now read from the section that publishes the band (§2 for `fast`, §3 for `invariant`, the same two sections the bands themselves are read from, so the scoping needs no new convention). Verified BOTH directions, which is what makes the red meaningful: moving `fast`'s derivation out of §2 to the end of the file is red under the new scoping and was GREEN under the old whole-file search. The helper falls back to the whole document if the headings ever move, because a scoping helper that silently matches NOTHING would turn item 5 (derivation) into a guaranteed red and get itself deleted — the failure mode this repo already had once with a `tasks/reviews` path prefix (PR #20 R20). T-R63's R22 residue is closed 2026-08-28, by removing the coupling rather than patching one direction of it. The §6-reference sweep read `region` — the text between the two markers — so every graded `§6 item N (slug)` citation depended on where the markers sat, and the 19 lines between the begin marker and the first pinned name are unpinned comment carrying two of them. Moving the begin marker down to `_BAND_LINE` left `marker_counts == [1, 1]`, `outside_the_region == []` and `markers_off_a_top_level_boundary == False` — green — while a reference corrupted inside those abandoned lines went from red to green. The markers exist to bound where band CODE may live, which is a different question from where a citation may be wrong: a `§6 item N` reference is wrong wherever it sits, so the sweep has no reason to be bounded at all. It now reads the whole file, which no marker move can narrow. Verified in BOTH directions with the block's own mutation — marker moved down AND `item 8 (references)` corrupted to `item 8 (wrong-slug)`: GREEN under the region-bounded sweep, RED under the file-wide one.

triage.note: tagged invariant. The cost is deliberate and is the same one `docs-numbers-are-derived` charges: a run slower than the published band reddens the next gate run until the band is re-measured, and adding a case to a suite reddens it until the band is re-measured at the new count. A band nobody re-measures is the thing that produced R21.
